questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The primary aim of agricultural research institutes in Nigeria is to
options: develop improved varieties, breeds and techniques for farmers
regulate the price of agricultural land
issue import licences for farm machinery
sell farm produce directly to the public
questions.explanation: Research institutes exist chiefly to generate improved crop varieties, animal breeds and farming techniques that extension services then pass on to farmers.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mixed farming, as a system of agriculture, involves the
options: cultivation of only one crop over a very large area
practice of shifting from one piece of land to another yearly
rearing of a single livestock species exclusively
combination of crop production and livestock rearing on the same farm
questions.explanation: Mixed farming integrates both crop and livestock enterprises on the same holding, allowing manure and crop residues to be exchanged between the two.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Monoculture, as practised in large plantations, refers to the
options: rearing of many different animal species together
practice of leaving land fallow for several years
continuous cultivation of a single crop on the same piece of land
rotation of several crops on the same land each season
questions.explanation: Monoculture is the repeated growing of one crop species on the same land, common on plantations such as oil palm or rubber estates.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Shifting cultivation is a traditional farming practice mainly associated with
options: greenhouse production of vegetables
clearing a plot, farming it briefly, then abandoning it for a fallow period
large mechanised farms in the savanna
the continuous use of a fixed plot with heavy fertiliser application
questions.explanation: Under shifting cultivation, a farmer clears and cultivates a plot for a few seasons, then abandons it to fallow while soil fertility is restored naturally.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Bush fallowing differs from shifting cultivation mainly in that, under bush fallowing, the
options: farmer abandons the homestead entirely and relocates with each new plot
same crop must be grown every season without exception
farmer's compound or homestead remains fixed while only the cultivated plot is rotated
land is never allowed a resting period
questions.explanation: In bush fallowing the farmstead stays put and only the farmed plots rotate through a fallow cycle, unlike shifting cultivation where the whole settlement may move.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a major reason for the low productivity of traditional agriculture in Nigeria?
options: Excessive use of certified improved seeds
Continued reliance on rudimentary tools and outdated methods
Overuse of modern irrigation systems
Widespread adoption of mechanised harvesters
questions.explanation: Traditional farming in many parts of Nigeria still depends on simple hand tools and age-old practices, limiting the scale and efficiency of output.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of these is classified as an arable crop?
options: Rubber
Oil palm
Maize
Cocoa
questions.explanation: Arable crops are those grown from seed and harvested within a season, such as maize, unlike tree or perennial crops like oil palm, cocoa and rubber.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A plantation crop is best described as one that is
options: harvested and replanted within a single farming season
grown exclusively for home consumption
cultivated only in greenhouses
a perennial crop grown on a large, continuous scale for commercial purposes
questions.explanation: Plantation crops such as rubber, oil palm and cocoa are perennial, long-term crops typically grown on a large commercial scale.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The term 'agroforestry' refers to a land-use system that
options: restricts land use strictly to forestry alone
combines the growing of trees with crops and/or livestock on the same land
involves clearing all trees before any cultivation begins
excludes livestock rearing from farmland entirely
questions.explanation: Agroforestry deliberately integrates trees with arable crops and sometimes livestock, providing complementary benefits such as shade, soil improvement and extra income.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: One major problem facing agricultural development in Nigeria is
options: too many trained agricultural extension officers
poor rural infrastructure such as roads, which hampers movement of produce
excessive government subsidy on farm inputs
an oversupply of agricultural credit to farmers
questions.explanation: Poor rural roads and storage facilities make it difficult and costly to move farm produce from rural areas to markets, discouraging productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Land tenure, in the context of Nigerian agriculture, refers to the
options: seasonal pattern of rainfall distribution
chemical composition of the topsoil
system by which land is owned, held and transferred
classification of crops by their growth habit
questions.explanation: Land tenure describes the rules and customs governing who owns land, how it is acquired, and how rights to it are passed on.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farm records are kept by a farm manager mainly to
options: replace the need for farm labour
eliminate all forms of farm risk
provide accurate information for planning, decision-making and evaluating performance
increase the physical size of the farm
questions.explanation: Farm records document inputs, outputs, costs and returns, giving the manager the data needed to plan future operations and assess profitability.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: An ecosystem, as studied in agricultural ecology, refers to the
options: process of breeding new plant varieties
classification of soil types found in a region
list of crops suited to a particular climate
interaction between living organisms and their non-living environment
questions.explanation: An ecosystem is a functional unit comprising living organisms (biotic) interacting with each other and with non-living (abiotic) factors like soil, water and air.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A food chain in an agro-ecosystem typically begins with
options: primary consumers, such as herbivores
decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi
producers, such as green plants, which trap solar energy
secondary consumers, such as carnivores
questions.explanation: Food chains start with producers (green plants) that convert solar energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis, forming the base of the chain.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Decomposers in an agricultural ecosystem play the important role of
options: preying directly on living herbivores
breaking down dead organic matter and releasing nutrients back into the soil
fixing atmospheric nitrogen exclusively
trapping solar energy for use by plants
questions.explanation: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead plant and animal matter, recycling nutrients back into the soil for uptake by producers.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A biotic factor affecting crop production in an ecosystem includes
options: the amount of rainfall received in a season
pests, diseases and weeds competing with or attacking the crop
the mineral composition of the soil
the intensity of sunlight reaching the crop
questions.explanation: Biotic factors are living components of the environment, such as pests, pathogens and weeds, that directly interact with and affect crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of an abiotic factor in agricultural ecology?
options: Soil temperature
A parasitic weed such as Striga
Population of soil earthworms
A herd of grazing cattle
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living physical or chemical components of the environment, such as temperature, rainfall, and soil pH.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ecological succession refers to the
options: sudden extinction of a single crop species
annual rotation of crops on a single plot
process of ploughing and harrowing farmland
gradual, orderly change in the composition of a plant community over time
questions.explanation: Ecological succession describes the progressive replacement of one plant community by another over time, eventually leading toward a stable climax community.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The derived savanna vegetation zone of Nigeria arose mainly as a result of
options: repeated human activities such as farming and bush burning degrading forest into grassland
volcanic activity destroying forest cover
permanent flooding of the rainforest belt
a naturally occurring desert expansion
questions.explanation: Derived savanna is a secondary vegetation type that resulted from continuous clearing, farming and burning of what was originally rainforest.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Symbiosis, as observed between rhizobium bacteria and leguminous plants, is best described as
options: a mutually beneficial relationship where both organisms gain from the association
a competitive relationship for the same limited resource
a relationship where one organism benefits and harms the other
a relationship where one organism benefits with no effect on the other
questions.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen for the legume's use, while the legume supplies the bacteria with carbohydrates, making it a mutualistic symbiosis.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Parasitism, as an ecological relationship affecting crops, describes a situation where one organism
options: competes with another for the same food source without direct contact
cooperates with another for mutual survival benefit
lives on or in another organism and derives nourishment at the host's expense
benefits from another without affecting it in any way
questions.explanation: In parasitism, the parasite obtains nutrients from a host organism, usually causing harm to the host, as seen with pests like aphids on crop plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Nitrogen fixation is the process by which
options: nitrogen is lost from the soil through leaching
atmospheric nitrogen gas is converted into a form usable by plants
soil nitrates are converted into nitrogen gas
plants release nitrogen gas back into the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation, carried out by certain bacteria, converts inert atmospheric nitrogen gas into compounds such as ammonia that plants can absorb and use.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Denitrification in the nitrogen cycle refers to the process by which
options: atmospheric nitrogen is converted into ammonia by bacteria
nitrates in the soil are converted back into atmospheric nitrogen gas
plants absorb nitrates directly from the soil
nitrites are converted into nitrates by nitrifying bacteria
questions.explanation: Denitrification is carried out by denitrifying bacteria under low-oxygen (waterlogged) conditions, converting soil nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which is lost to the atmosphere.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Wind, as an ecological factor, affects crop production mainly by
options: determining the pH level of the soil
directly increasing the nitrogen content of the soil
increasing the rate of transpiration and potentially causing lodging in tall crops
controlling the length of the rainy season
questions.explanation: Strong winds raise the rate of water loss (transpiration) from leaves and can physically knock down or lodge tall-stemmed crops such as maize.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A disc plough is generally preferred over a mouldboard plough for primary tillage on
options: wetland rice fields exclusively
soils that require no inversion at all
very loose, sandy soils with no obstructions
hard, dry or stony soils, where it can cut through with less clogging
questions.explanation: Disc ploughs are well suited to hard, dry, stony or root-infested soils because their rotating discs cut through obstructions with far less clogging than a mouldboard plough.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A seed drill is a farm implement used mainly for
options: planting seeds at a uniform depth and spacing in rows
harvesting mature cereal crops
spraying herbicides on standing crops
threshing grain after harvest
questions.explanation: A seed drill sows seeds mechanically at a controlled depth and even row spacing, improving on the unevenness of broadcasting by hand.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A sprayer is a piece of farm equipment specifically designed to
options: till and pulverise the soil before planting
apply liquid chemicals such as pesticides and herbicides to crops
measure the moisture content of harvested grain
cut and gather mature grain crops
questions.explanation: Sprayers are used to apply liquid agrochemicals, such as insecticides, fungicides and herbicides, evenly over crops or fields.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The main purpose of a farm silo is to
options: till the soil before planting
irrigate crops during the dry season
harvest root and tuber crops
store bulk feed or grain under conditions that limit spoilage
questions.explanation: A silo is a storage structure designed to keep grain or silage in bulk while protecting it from moisture, pests and spoilage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A wheelbarrow used on the farm is best classified as a
options: primary tillage implement
type of irrigation equipment
simple hand tool for conveying farm materials over short distances
mechanised harvesting machine
questions.explanation: The wheelbarrow is a manually operated hand tool used to transport materials such as soil, manure or harvested produce over short distances.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following safety practices is most important when operating a farm tractor?
options: Removing the safety guard to increase visibility
Operating the tractor at maximum speed at all times
Ensuring all guards are in place and avoiding loose clothing near moving parts
Allowing untrained persons to operate the machine for practice
questions.explanation: Keeping protective guards in place and avoiding loose clothing near power take-off shafts and other moving parts is essential to prevent serious tractor-related accidents.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Land clearing, as a farm operation, involves the
options: removal of trees, stumps and vegetation to prepare land for cultivation
sorting and grading of farm produce
application of fertiliser to growing crops
harvesting of mature farm produce
questions.explanation: Land clearing is the initial operation of removing unwanted trees, shrubs, stumps and debris so that the land can subsequently be tilled and planted.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ridging, as a farm operation, is particularly beneficial for crops such as yam mainly because it
options: increases the nitrogen content of the topsoil directly
provides loose, well-aerated soil for good tuber development and improves drainage
reduces the amount of sunlight reaching the crop
eliminates the need for weeding throughout the season
questions.explanation: Ridges create a deep, loose, well-drained soil mass that allows tubers like yam to expand freely while also channelling away excess water.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: An animal-drawn implement such as an ox-plough is most suited to farmers who
options: operate very large mechanised commercial plantations
cannot afford a tractor but require more power than manual hand tools provide
require precision planting of tree seedlings only
farm exclusively in greenhouse conditions
questions.explanation: Animal traction, such as ox-drawn ploughs, offers small-scale farmers a level of power between manual hand tools and costly tractors.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a key advantage of mechanised farming over the exclusive use of hand tools?
options: It removes the need for any form of maintenance
It guarantees higher soil fertility automatically
It allows a larger area of land to be cultivated within a shorter time
It always eliminates the need for skilled labour entirely
questions.explanation: Mechanisation increases the speed and scale of farm operations, enabling more land to be worked in less time compared to manual labour alone.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Threshing, as a post-harvest operation, refers to the
options: storage of grain in airtight containers
drying of harvested produce under the sun
cutting and gathering of a mature crop from the field
separation of grain from the straw or husk after harvesting
questions.explanation: Threshing is the operation that separates the edible grain from the straw, stalks or husks after the crop has been reaped.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The main function of a planter (mechanical planting machine) on a mechanised farm is to
options: place seeds at the correct depth and spacing in one continuous operation
apply irrigation water to the field
harvest and thresh grain crops simultaneously
remove weeds from between crop rows
questions.explanation: A mechanical planter opens the furrow, drops the seed at a set spacing and depth, and covers it, all in a single continuous pass.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil is best defined as the
options: hard rock layer found deep beneath the earth's surface
loose surface layer of the earth's crust that supports plant growth
body of water found in rivers and lakes
gaseous layer surrounding the earth
questions.explanation: Soil is the thin, loose, weathered layer covering the earth's surface, formed from rock and organic material, capable of supporting plant life.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Sandy soil is characterised mainly by
options: large particle size, good drainage, and low water-holding capacity
the highest nutrient-retention capacity among soil types
a sticky texture when wet and poor drainage
very small particle size and high water-holding capacity
questions.explanation: Sandy soils have coarse, large particles with wide pore spaces, giving them excellent drainage but a poor ability to retain water and nutrients.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Clay soil is generally less favourable for root crop production mainly because it
options: has particles too large for roots to penetrate
becomes compact and waterlogged, restricting root expansion and aeration
contains too little organic matter to support any growth
drains water too quickly for roots to absorb
questions.explanation: Clay soils have very fine particles that pack tightly, holding excess water and limiting the aeration and expansion space that root and tuber crops need.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Loam soil is generally considered the most suitable soil type for crop production because it
options: consists almost entirely of large sand particles
combines good drainage, aeration and water/nutrient retention
is composed purely of decomposed organic matter
has no mineral particles present at all
questions.explanation: Loam is a balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay that provides good drainage and aeration while still retaining adequate moisture and nutrients.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil texture refers to the
options: acidity or alkalinity level of the soil
amount of organic matter present in the soil
relative proportion of sand, silt and clay particles in the soil
arrangement of soil particles into aggregates or crumbs
questions.explanation: Soil texture is determined by the relative percentages of sand, silt and clay-sized mineral particles that make up the soil.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil structure, as distinct from soil texture, refers to the
options: way individual soil particles are arranged or aggregated together
depth of the topsoil layer
proportion of sand, silt and clay in the soil
chemical elements dissolved in the soil water
questions.explanation: Soil structure describes how individual soil particles clump or bind together into aggregates, which affects aeration, drainage and root penetration.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil pH is a measure of the
options: moisture-holding capacity of the soil
total mineral content of the soil
amount of organic matter present in the soil
degree of acidity or alkalinity of the soil
questions.explanation: Soil pH indicates how acidic or alkaline the soil is on a scale, which strongly influences nutrient availability to plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Most arable crops grow best within a soil pH range that is
options: extremely acidic, below 3.0
completely neutral at exactly 14.0
slightly acidic to neutral, roughly 6.0 to 7.0
extremely alkaline, above 9.0
questions.explanation: Most crop nutrients are most readily available to plants in a slightly acidic to neutral pH range, approximately 6.0 to 7.0.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Liming is a soil management practice carried out mainly to
options: eliminate all organic matter from the soil
increase the sand content of the soil
reduce soil acidity by raising the pH of acidic soils
reduce the water-holding capacity of the soil
questions.explanation: Applying lime to acidic soils neutralises excess acidity, raising the pH to a range more favourable for nutrient availability and crop growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Organic matter improves soil fertility mainly by
options: increasing the proportion of sand particles in the soil
lowering the soil pH to extremely acidic levels
reducing the population of beneficial soil microorganisms
improving soil structure, water retention and supplying nutrients as it decomposes
questions.explanation: Decomposing organic matter binds soil particles into stable aggregates, improves water-holding capacity, and releases nutrients as it breaks down.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Humus refers to the
options: topmost living vegetation covering the soil
dark, well-decomposed organic material in the soil
layer of solid rock beneath the soil profile
mineral fraction of the soil derived from parent rock
questions.explanation: Humus is the stable, dark-coloured, well-decomposed organic material remaining after plant and animal residues have broken down.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cover cropping helps to control soil erosion mainly by
options: compacting the soil to prevent water infiltration
shielding the soil surface from the direct impact of rain and wind
increasing the slope of the farmland
removing all organic matter from the topsoil
questions.explanation: A cover crop's foliage intercepts raindrops and reduces wind speed at the soil surface, protecting the topsoil from being dislodged and washed or blown away.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The three main components of a fertile agricultural soil profile, from top to bottom, are generally described as the
options: topsoil, subsoil and parent material
sand, silt and clay layers
root zone, stem zone and canopy zone
humus, water and air layers
questions.explanation: A typical soil profile is divided into distinct horizons, broadly the nutrient-rich topsoil, the subsoil beneath it, and the parent material or bedrock below.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Leaching, as a process affecting soil fertility, refers to the
options: upward movement of nutrients to the soil surface
addition of fertiliser nutrients to the topsoil
downward movement and loss of soluble nutrients beyond the reach of plant roots
conversion of organic matter into humus
questions.explanation: Leaching occurs when excess water percolating through the soil carries dissolved nutrients down past the root zone, making them unavailable to crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following soil organisms is most beneficial in improving soil aeration and structure?
options: Fungal pathogen causing root rot
Earthworm
Termite that attacks crop roots
Nematode pest
questions.explanation: Earthworms burrow through the soil, creating channels that improve aeration and drainage, while their casts enrich the soil with nutrients.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Crop rotation is a farming practice that involves
options: planting several crops together at random on one plot
growing the same crop continuously on the same land every season
growing different crops in a planned sequence on the same land over successive seasons
abandoning farmland permanently after one season of use
questions.explanation: Crop rotation deliberately alternates different crop types on the same plot across seasons to maintain soil fertility and disrupt pest and disease cycles.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: One major benefit of including a leguminous crop in a crop rotation programme is that it
options: requires no sunlight to grow successfully
depletes soil nitrogen faster than other crops
eliminates the need for any weeding
helps restore soil nitrogen through its nitrogen-fixing root nodules
questions.explanation: Legumes host nitrogen-fixing rhizobium bacteria in their root nodules, which convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form that enriches the soil for subsequent crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mixed cropping refers to the practice of
options: growing two or more crops simultaneously on the same piece of land
growing a single crop species over a very large area
rotating a single crop with a fallow period only
leaving farmland completely fallow for a long period
questions.explanation: Mixed cropping involves cultivating more than one crop species together on the same plot at the same time, often to maximise land use and reduce risk.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A major advantage of mixed cropping over monocropping is that it
options: eliminates competition between crops entirely
guarantees a higher yield of every individual crop grown
requires no knowledge of individual crop requirements
reduces the overall risk of total crop failure and makes efficient use of land resources
questions.explanation: By growing several crops together, a farmer spreads risk since a pest, disease or price failure affecting one crop is unlikely to affect all the crops equally.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Seed dormancy refers to a condition in which a viable seed
options: loses its ability to germinate permanently
fails to germinate even under otherwise favourable conditions
germinates immediately once planted
is destroyed by pests before planting
questions.explanation: A dormant seed is alive and capable of germinating but remains inactive under favourable conditions until an internal or external barrier to germination is removed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a recognised method of breaking seed dormancy before planting?
options: Storing the seed at extremely high temperatures indefinitely
Continuous flooding of the seed for several months
Scarification of the hard seed coat
Coating the seed entirely in wax
questions.explanation: Scarification, scratching or nicking a hard seed coat, allows water and oxygen to penetrate, breaking dormancy caused by impermeable seed coats.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The correct planting depth for a seed is generally guided by the
options: colour of the seed coat
size of the seed, with larger seeds typically planted deeper
distance of the farm from the nearest town
market price of the resulting produce
questions.explanation: As a general agronomic guideline, larger seeds with greater food reserves are planted deeper, while small seeds are planted shallowly, close to the surface.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mulching is a crop management practice that involves
options: removing all vegetation cover from the soil surface
digging deep trenches around each plant
burning plant residues on the field before planting
covering the soil surface around plants with organic or other material
questions.explanation: Mulching spreads a protective layer, often organic material like straw, over the soil surface around crops to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: One major benefit of mulching to a growing crop is that it
options: increases the rate of soil erosion
eliminates the need for any irrigation permanently
conserves soil moisture and suppresses weed growth
reduces the organic matter content of the soil
questions.explanation: By covering bare soil, mulch reduces evaporation losses and blocks light needed by weed seeds to germinate, benefiting the main crop.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weeds are generally undesirable on farmland mainly because they
options: increase the market value of the harvested crop
always improve the fertility of the soil
attract beneficial pollinators exclusively
compete with crops for nutrients, water, light and space
questions.explanation: Weeds are unwanted plants that compete directly with cultivated crops for essential growth resources, often reducing crop yield if left unchecked.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a chemical method of weed control?
options: Hoeing between crop rows
Crop rotation with a smothering cover crop
Application of a selective herbicide
Hand-pulling of weeds
questions.explanation: Herbicides are chemical substances applied specifically to kill or suppress weeds, distinguishing chemical control from manual or cultural methods.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Crop pests differ from crop pathogens mainly in that pests are generally
options: microscopic disease-causing organisms like bacteria, fungi and viruses
beneficial organisms that always aid pollination
visible organisms, such as insects and rodents, that directly damage the crop
chemicals applied to protect the crop
questions.explanation: Pests are typically larger, often visible organisms such as insects, rodents and birds, whereas pathogens are microscopic disease-causing agents like fungi, bacteria and viruses.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is best described as an approach that
options: focuses only on the use of resistant crop varieties
eliminates all pest control practices from farming
combines biological, cultural, chemical and other control methods for sustainable pest control
relies exclusively on the heavy use of chemical pesticides
questions.explanation: IPM integrates multiple complementary strategies, biological, cultural, mechanical and judicious chemical control, to manage pests sustainably and minimise resistance and environmental harm.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Biological control of crop pests involves the use of
options: resistant crop varieties bred through hybridisation
natural enemies, such as predators or parasites, to reduce pest populations
synthetic chemical pesticides sprayed on the crop
physical barriers like fences around the farm
questions.explanation: Biological control harnesses natural enemies of a pest, such as predatory insects or parasitic wasps, to keep pest populations in check without chemicals.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Harvesting a crop before it reaches full maturity generally results in
options: reduced yield and poorer quality of the produce
higher nutrient content in the harvested produce
an automatic increase in the crop's market value
improved storage life of the harvested produce
questions.explanation: Premature harvesting typically means the crop has not accumulated its full potential yield or quality, resulting in smaller, less developed produce.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Curing, as applied to harvested tubers such as yam, is carried out mainly to
options: heal surface wounds and toughen the skin to reduce storage losses
increase the moisture content of the tuber before storage
artificially ripen the tuber for immediate consumption
remove all starch content from the tuber
questions.explanation: Curing allows harvested tubers to heal cuts and bruises and develop a tougher outer skin, which reduces rot and water loss during storage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Grading of harvested farm produce refers to the
options: application of chemicals to preserve produce
sorting of produce into different categories based on quality, size or maturity
process of drying produce under direct sunlight
transportation of produce from the farm to the market
questions.explanation: Grading separates farm produce into defined classes based on attributes such as size, quality or ripeness, which helps in pricing and marketing.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Animal husbandry is best defined as the branch of agriculture concerned with the
options: cultivation and management of crops for human consumption
marketing and distribution of farm produce
study of soil formation and classification
breeding, feeding, housing and general management of farm animals
questions.explanation: Animal husbandry covers all aspects of raising livestock, including breeding, nutrition, housing, health and general management practices.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is classified as a monogastric farm animal?
options: Cattle
Goat
Pig
Sheep
questions.explanation: The pig has a single-chambered stomach, classifying it as monogastric, unlike ruminants such as cattle, sheep and goats, which have a multi-chambered stomach.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ruminant animals, such as cattle and goats, are distinguished from monogastric animals by having
options: a single-chambered stomach with limited fibre digestion ability
a digestive system identical to that of poultry
no stomach at all in their digestive system
a four-chambered stomach adapted for digesting fibrous plant material
questions.explanation: Ruminants possess a specialised four-compartment stomach (rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum) that allows efficient breakdown of fibrous, cellulose-rich feed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The rumen, the largest chamber of a ruminant's stomach, functions mainly as a
options: chamber that filters blood before digestion
structure used solely for water storage
site where milk is produced and stored
fermentation chamber where microorganisms break down fibrous feed
questions.explanation: The rumen houses billions of microorganisms that ferment and break down cellulose and other fibrous plant materials the animal itself cannot digest directly.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Colostrum, the first milk produced by a mammal after giving birth, is especially important to the newborn because it
options: is harmful and should be withheld from the newborn
contains no nutritional value whatsoever
is produced only in animals that do not suckle their young
provides antibodies that boost the newborn's immunity against disease
questions.explanation: Colostrum is rich in maternal antibodies that give the newborn passive immunity, protecting it from disease during its first vulnerable weeks of life.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Culling, as a livestock management practice, refers to the
options: housing of animals in a well-ventilated structure
process of feeding animals a balanced ration
removal of unproductive or undesirable animals from the herd or flock
vaccination of animals against common diseases
questions.explanation: Culling involves identifying and removing animals that are unproductive, diseased or otherwise undesirable, improving the overall quality and efficiency of the remaining herd or flock.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Castration of male farm animals not intended for breeding is carried out mainly to
options: make the animals calmer and improve the quality of meat produced
prevent the animals from ever gaining weight
increase their fertility for breeding purposes
eliminate the need for proper feeding
questions.explanation: Castration removes the testes, reducing aggressive behaviour and often improving growth rate and meat quality in animals raised specifically for meat.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of an intensive system of livestock management?
options: Battery cage system for layers
Free-range system for poultry
Ranching system for beef cattle
Nomadic pastoral system for cattle
questions.explanation: The battery cage system confines birds closely in cages within a controlled structure, representing a highly intensive form of poultry management.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Extensive livestock management, such as free-range grazing, is characterised mainly by
options: animals roaming over a large area to source most of their own feed
complete control over every aspect of feeding and breeding
animals being confined entirely within small cages
the highest possible stocking density per unit area
questions.explanation: In extensive systems, animals graze freely over wide areas, obtaining most of their feed naturally, with comparatively little direct human control.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Artificial insemination in livestock breeding involves the
options: cloning of an animal from a single somatic cell
introduction of collected semen into a female's reproductive tract by artificial means
natural mating of a male and female of the same species
surgical removal of reproductive organs from breeding stock
questions.explanation: Artificial insemination allows semen collected from a superior male to be introduced into the female reproductive tract without natural mating, spreading desirable genetics widely.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A major advantage of artificial insemination in livestock improvement is that it
options: eliminates the need for any record-keeping on the farm
removes the need for proper animal nutrition entirely
guarantees that every offspring produced will be female
allows the genes of a superior male to be used to breed many females widely
questions.explanation: Because semen from one outstanding male can be distributed to inseminate numerous females, artificial insemination rapidly spreads valuable genetic traits across a population.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following nutrients is the primary source of energy in a typical livestock ration?
options: Water
Vitamins
Carbohydrates
Minerals
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates, found abundantly in feeds such as maize and other cereals, serve as the main dietary source of energy for farm animals.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Protein in a livestock ration is especially important mainly because it
options: supports growth, tissue repair and the building of body structures
prevents all forms of livestock disease automatically
is the animal's primary source of immediate energy
regulates the animal's body temperature directly
questions.explanation: Proteins supply the amino acids needed for building and repairing muscle and other body tissues, making them essential for growth and productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A balanced ration for livestock is best described as a feed mixture that
options: consists entirely of water with no solid feed
contains only a single feed ingredient
supplies all required nutrients in the correct proportion and quantity for a given animal
is composed purely of minerals with no energy source
questions.explanation: A balanced ration is carefully formulated to provide the right amounts and proportions of energy, protein, vitamins and minerals needed by a particular class of livestock.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Foot-and-mouth disease is a major infectious disease that primarily affects
options: rabbits and other small mammals only
fish in freshwater ponds only
poultry exclusively
cloven-hoofed animals such as cattle, sheep, goats and pigs
questions.explanation: Foot-and-mouth disease is a highly contagious viral disease that specifically affects cloven-hoofed livestock, causing blisters on the mouth and feet.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Newcastle disease is a major viral disease of significant economic importance in
options: cattle
sheep
pigs
poultry
questions.explanation: Newcastle disease is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease affecting domestic poultry, causing significant economic losses if not controlled through vaccination.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Vaccination of livestock is carried out mainly to
options: improve the taste of meat produced by the animal
eliminate the need for proper feeding and housing
increase the animal's body weight directly
stimulate the animal's immune system to develop resistance against specific diseases
questions.explanation: Vaccines expose an animal's immune system to a weakened or inactivated pathogen, prompting it to develop protective antibodies against future infection by that disease.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an important factor to consider when selecting a site for livestock housing?
options: Good drainage and adequate ventilation of the site
Proximity to a densely populated residential estate
Absence of any access road to the site
A site permanently prone to flooding
questions.explanation: A well-drained, well-ventilated site helps keep livestock housing dry and free of excess moisture, reducing disease risk and improving animal comfort.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ectoparasites, such as ticks and mites, are external parasites of livestock that mainly cause harm by
options: improving the animal's overall growth rate
feeding on blood or skin, leading to irritation, blood loss and disease transmission
living entirely within the animal's digestive tract
providing essential nutrients to the host animal
questions.explanation: Ectoparasites attach to the animal's skin, feeding on blood or tissue, which causes irritation, blood loss, reduced productivity, and can transmit disease-causing organisms.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weaning, in livestock management, refers to the
options: process of vaccinating a newborn animal
gradual withdrawal of a young animal from dependence on its mother's milk
castration of a young male animal
process of selecting breeding stock for mating
questions.explanation: Weaning is the transitional process of shifting a young animal's diet away from milk and onto solid feed, ending its dependence on the mother.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Fish farming, or aquaculture, is best defined as the
options: rearing of birds in an enclosed poultry house
harvesting of wild fish from natural rivers and oceans
cultivation of crops on flooded farmland
deliberate rearing of fish and other aquatic organisms under controlled conditions
questions.explanation: Aquaculture involves the intentional breeding, stocking and management of fish and other aquatic species in ponds or tanks, distinct from capturing wild fish.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A concrete or earthen fish pond used in aquaculture must have a reliable water supply mainly to
options: prevent the fish from ever reproducing
increase the amount of feed the fish consume
maintain suitable water quality and quantity for fish growth and survival
eliminate the need to feed the fish at all
questions.explanation: A steady, adequate water supply is essential in a fish pond to sustain proper oxygen levels, temperature and overall water quality needed for healthy fish growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural economics is best described as the branch of agriculture concerned with the
options: classification and management of soil types
breeding and genetic improvement of farm animals
study of pest and disease control on crops
application of economic principles to farm production, resource use and marketing decisions
questions.explanation: Agricultural economics applies core economic principles, such as scarcity, cost and efficient resource allocation, to decisions about farm production and marketing.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A farm budget is best described as a
options: record of past weather patterns affecting a farm
schedule of vaccination dates for farm animals
list of livestock breeds kept on a farm
plan estimating expected income and expenditure for a farm business over a period
questions.explanation: A farm budget forecasts anticipated revenues and costs for a defined period, helping the farmer plan resource allocation and assess likely profitability.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Fixed costs in farm production are costs that
options: are incurred exclusively when produce is sold
occur only once during the entire life of the farm business
vary directly and proportionately with the level of output produced
remain constant regardless of the level of output produced
questions.explanation: Fixed costs, such as land rent or depreciation on buildings, must be paid whether output is high, low, or even zero, and do not change with production level.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Variable costs in farm production include expenses such as
options: cost of seeds, fertiliser and labour, which change with the level of output
insurance premiums paid once a year regardless of output
depreciation on permanent farm buildings
annual land rent, which stays the same regardless of output
questions.explanation: Variable costs, such as seed, fertiliser and hired labour, rise or fall directly with the scale of production undertaken.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farm profit is calculated as the
options: total land area under cultivation on the farm
difference between total farm revenue and total farm costs
sum of all fixed and variable costs incurred
total quantity of produce harvested in a season
questions.explanation: Profit is the financial surplus remaining after all costs (fixed and variable) have been subtracted from the total revenue earned from the farm business.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The law of diminishing returns, as applied in agriculture, states that beyond a certain point
options: every additional unit of input always increases output by the same amount
output continues to rise indefinitely as more input is added
reducing an input always increases total output
additional units of a variable input yield progressively smaller increases in output
questions.explanation: The law of diminishing returns describes how, once an optimal input level is passed, each extra unit of a variable input adds progressively less to total output.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Demand for a farm product, in economic terms, refers to the
options: quantity of the product buyers are willing and able to purchase at a given price
government-imposed price ceiling on the product
total quantity of the product available for sale in the market
amount of the product that farmers wish to produce
questions.explanation: Demand specifically describes the quantity consumers are both willing and financially able to buy at a particular price, not merely a general desire for the good.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Supply of a farm product refers to the
options: total land area used to cultivate the product
amount of a product lost to pests during storage
quantity of the product that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price
quantity of the product consumers wish to purchase at a given price
questions.explanation: Supply describes the quantity that sellers or producers are willing and able to bring to market for sale at a specified price.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Market equilibrium price is the price at which the
options: quantity supplied is always greater than the quantity demanded
government fixes the price regardless of demand or supply
quantity demanded of a product equals the quantity supplied
quantity demanded is always greater than the quantity supplied
questions.explanation: Equilibrium price occurs where the quantity buyers wish to purchase exactly matches the quantity sellers are willing to supply, clearing the market.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural marketing encompasses all the activities involved in
options: growing crops from planting to harvest only
breeding and selecting superior livestock
moving farm produce from the point of production to the final consumer
controlling pests and diseases on the farm
questions.explanation: Agricultural marketing covers the entire chain of activities, assembling, grading, storage, transport and sale, that gets produce from farm to consumer.
